World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Green light for Andrew Forrest's $70m Ningaloo Reef resort
World.content:
Mining billionaire Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest's plan for a $70 million luxury resort on the Ningaloo Reef has cleared its final approval hurdle, after years of delays and cutbacks.

In 2017, the Ningaloo Lighthouse Resort property, about 1,230 kilometres north of Perth, was snapped up by the magnate, who aimed to redevelop a rundown Exmouth caravan park at the site into an eco-tourism hotspot.

But the initial application to build an $85 million, 550-guest retreat was withdrawn while awaiting environmental and cultural approvals.

Nearly a decade passed while efforts to give the resort unfettered beach access were dumped by WA's Main Roads authority over fears it could damage an Aboriginal heritage site.

Andrew Forrest first submitted plans for the Ningaloo Reef site in 2017. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

A revised approach, submitted earlier this year to the local shire, reduced its footprint by $15 million dollars and about 400 guests.

The application was unanimously approved today by the WA Planning Commission, with minor amendments.

It is understood Z1Z Resorts, the accommodation arm of Andrew and Nicola Forrest's Tattarang company, is still working through the conditions in detail but has voiced a willingness to accept the changes before the assessment panel.

A spokesperson for the project could not confirm a timeframe for construction or opening.

"We look forward to working with the community as the project progresses," the spokesperson said.

Environmental concerns

The larger vision for the resort was given the green light by then WA Environment Minister Reece Whitby in 2023, subject to strict measures to protect wildlife and Aboriginal cultural sites.

At the time, the Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) recommended special lighting arrangements to minimise its impact on the sea turtles and shorebirds that lay their eggs along the World Heritage-listed Ningaloo coast.

The project, situated outside Exmouth and adjacent to the marine park, is unlikely to be assessed by the EPA again, as it has only decreased in size.

Current plans involve converting the heritage-listed Vlamingh Head lighthouse keepers' quarters into a hotel reception and constructing dozens of villas, a restaurant, and spa facilities.

A concept image of the Ningaloo Lighthouse Resort. (Supplied: Tattarang)

Almost four hectares of native vegetation will be cleared within the 45-hectare development.

The property still falls within a registered Aboriginal heritage area, Vlamingh Head, that has been a ceremonial and spiritual site for tens of thousands of years.

In its submission before the planning commission, Z1Z Resorts said it had obtained approval from the minister for Aboriginal affairs under Section 18 of Aboriginal Heritage Act 1972, and was consulting extensively with traditional owners.

Australian Marine Conservation Society chief executive Paul Gamblin previously opposed the development, but said it was now "heading in the right direction".

The Ningaloo Lighthouse Resort hopes to source potable water for the villas and plunge pools via groundwater bores, while wastewater will be recycled to irrigate the property.

The proposal fuelled unease for the region's already depleted groundwater stores and the fragile subterranean ecosystems that course through the limestone peninsula.

"If the current proposal stays within the existing footprint … but then also adopts contemporary energy and water efficient processes, and they should be absolutely world leading for an area like this, then that would be the appropriate approach," Mr Gamblin said.

Boost for cyclone-hit town

Exmouth Chamber of Commerce president David Gillespie also had groundwater concerns.

The state-run Water Corporation announced last year it would construct a seawater desalination plant in Exmouth by 2030, with the local drinking water scheme already approaching capacity.

"They've certainly got challenges around the infrastructure domain," Mr Gillespie said.

" It's just a matter of just how much money you throw at it to make it work. "

The tourist town of Exmouth in WA's north-west. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Mr Gillespie said it was a welcome economic reprieve for Exmouth, which was still recovering from ex-Tropical Cyclone Narelle.

The category-four system made landfall over Exmouth in March, wrecking a huge swathe of homes and businesses, including its largest resort.

"Less beds is putting more stress on the other accommodators (sic) to accommodate everybody at this point in time," Mr Gillespie said.

"Exmouth itself is going to take at least 18 months to two years just to get back to some normality."

The controversial miner is no stranger to the town, having opened a multi-million-dollar marine research facility there in 2021.

"Once it's built and it's open for business, it doesn't matter who owns it, it will be a great asset to Exmouth," Mr Gillespie said.

World.title: Labor's 'jaw dropping' fracking decision wedges One Nation at first opportunity
World.content:
Since One Nation's breakthrough state election result in South Australia this year, Premier Peter Malinauskas has been striking a seemingly diplomatic tone about parliament's new conservative cohort.

Last Tuesday, as South Australia's seven new One Nation MPs prepared for their first day in parliament, the Labor premier said we should "welcome the fact that there are opposition parties in our state who have an important function to perform to hold us to account".

"I stand ready willing and able to work with opposition parties regardless of their political hue, regardless of our political differences, if it's in the best interests of the state," he said at the time.

"I've communicated that to [One Nation SA leader] Cory [Bernardi] directly."

High-minded civics, sure.

A sign that Labor will make One Nation's life easy in parliament? Absolutely not.

Just ask new One Nation MP Jason Virgo.

One Nation's Jason Virgo won the seat of MacKillop in a contest with the Liberal Party. (Facebook: Jason Virgo for MacKillop)

The South East MP has just been put into a political bind by the government's push to end the moratorium on fracking in his local electorate.

The 10-year ban was legislated by the former Marshall Liberal government in 2018 in response to community fears the gas extraction method would threaten groundwater and local agriculture.

Those community concerns have not dissipated, but neither has One Nation's zest for resource extraction.

Last month national One Nation party leader Pauline Hanson was spruiking "drill, baby, drill" on social media.

It leaves One Nation having to balance its traditional views with those of Mr Virgo's constituents.

Peter Malinauskas (right) greets One Nation's new MPs on the first day of parliament. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Labor, which argues ending the moratorium can be done safely and is necessary to shore up gas supplies in the 2030s, will accuse One Nation and the Liberals of being energy hypocrites if they keep the moratorium in place.

"The Liberal Party and One Nation talk a big game when it comes to energy sovereignty and security — well, now they have an opportunity to prove it," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Instead, I fear they may hide behind the veil of confrontation."

But the level of community angst will be hard for Mr Virgo to ignore.

Naracoorte-Lucindale Mayor Patrick Ross said his "jaw dropped" when he heard the government's plan, and he is already making his views known to the fledgling One Nation MP.

"I've made it very clear, and I know that other mayors in the seat of MacKillop have made it very clear, that first and foremost you must represent your constituents," Mr Ross said.

Naracoorte Lucindale Mayor Patrick Ross says "fracking is a no go". (ABC News)

"It doesn't matter where the party may sit [or] One Nation may sit on resources extraction, you must support the people who put you into the parliament, and that is the constituents.

"And they will be very loud and clear to Jason Virgo that fracking is a no-go for MacKillop."

An attempt at the middle path

Mr Virgo has already tried to find middle ground through the issue, calling for local consultation.

In a rare interview with 891 ABC Adelaide today, he said the moratorium was ending in 2028 so "there's no need to push it through today or next week".

One Nation's Jason Virgo Sixteen years before Jason Virgo won the SA seat of MacKillop for One Nation in the state's south-east, he twice ran for parliament as an Australian Sex Party candidate.

"Our community down here really wanted the country cabinet to come down and listen to the concerns that are facing our region, and instead what we've had is a bit of a slap in the face," he said.

Mr Virgo, who rejected that he was trying to walk on both sides of the street, said the eastern states should play a bigger role in gas extraction.

"Gas security is important and there is plenty of the state to drill for gas, we absolutely want gas," he said.

"But what I would suggest is that the Labor premier needs to get onto his Labor mates in the eastern states and get them to start drilling their fair share."

Liberal MLC Ben Hood, from Mount Gambier, made a similar call for consultation, while federal Liberal MP Tony Pasin told the premier to "frack off".

A second environmental battle

There are risks for Labor, too.

Ministers could face some fiery criticism as they try to explain their decision at a country cabinet forum in the South East tonight.

The move also draws attention to Labor's previous comments that it would not touch the fracking moratorium before 2028.

New independent Mount Gambier MP Travis Fatchen has already vowed to fight the proposal "every step of the way".

"Before the election in 2022, the premier gave a clear assurance to the people of the Limestone Coast that there would be no changes to the moratorium," he said.

"That promise has now been broken."

But Labor does not have much to lose in the South East either; the party has not held the seat of MacKillop since 1956 or Mount Gambier since 1975.

It is harder to imagine Labor wading into such a fraught environmental issue if they had a local MP fighting for re-election or were a realistic chance of winning a South East seat in 2030.

But it is also true that the government is fighting a separate environmental battle in an area where it does have a political stake.

One protester covered their face with a Peter Malinauskas mask and held a cardboard chainsaw at a protest earlier in the week. (ABC News: Angelique Donnellan)

That is the seat of Adelaide, where debate continues to rage over the felling of 585 trees in the parklands for the government's $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide golf course.

Rather than One Nation, this political fight has been with the Greens, with thousands gathering on the steps of Parliament House last night to protest the redevelopment.

Nothing has put the government off course so far and the trees continue to come down. The premier is pointing to Labor's resounding victory in the seat of Adelaide as a mandate.

One Nation wedged, the Greens steamrolled and the Liberals struggling for oxygen?

It could be an indicator of the next four years to come.

World.title: Business opposes Coalition plan to cut migration to meet housing needs
World.content:
Business groups have expressed concerns over the Coalition's proposal to significantly lower net overseas migration numbers.

"We have the numbers now on skilled migration about right," Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox told the ABC.

The Australian Industry Group (AiG) is the peak industry association, with a strong representation in the manufacturing sector.

"The focus needs to be on ensuring we are bringing the right skills to Australia when they are needed in a timely and efficient manner," Mr Willox said.

Economists divided on property prices Some economists are forecasting price falls of up to 5 per cent as a result of measures to reduce intergenerational housing inequality.

Net overseas migration is the net gain or loss of population through international migration to and from Australia.

In the year ending June 30, 2025, overseas migration contributed a net gain of 306,000 people to Australia's population, according to ABS data.

This was a decrease from the net gain of 429,000 people the previous year, and below the financial year record of 538,000 people in 2022-23.

"It will be more than 70 per cent below that peak," Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told Seven's Sunrise.

"But let me tell you, it will be in line with the houses available and we will assess each year what houses we have in this country and that will provide a cap to the people who come into this country.

"We cannot have young Australians who are missing out on getting into a home because the level of migration is too high."

Loading

Open to debate on migration

The Coalition wants to limit Australia's net migration intake to only one person per new home built, but will wait until it is in government to decide what visa types to slash if elected.

Mr Willox said he was open to a debate on migration "as it is a key driver of our economic fortunes."

However, he said, maintaining the focus on a transparent and responsive skilled migration program as a key part of the overall program was "sacrosanct".

Mr Willox said he saw migration as an essential lever in managing Australia's supply response as demand changed in the economy.

"Skilled migration is vital in plugging gaps, developing skills and helping businesses grow and adapt to changing circumstances when the domestic economy can't meet market needs or changing conditions," Mr Willox said.

The average Australian household dwelling houses 2.6 people, but the Coalition's policy would allow net migration to grow at a ratio of one person to one home built.

The Coalition said that would give the construction sector time to "catch up" after historically high net overseas migration (NOM) in recent years.

The Coalition wants to tie migration to housing supply. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mr Taylor said under Labor migration had run "miles ahead" of housing.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) acting chief executive, David Alexander, has also weighed into the migration debate.

"It's very important that policymakers get the design of our migration policy right because a well-designed migration program can bring significant economic benefits to Australia," Mr Alexander said.

" The migration program needs to be balanced and sustainable to ensure both public support and broader economic benefits. "

Mr Alexander said policy makers needed to consider a range of elements in the consideration of net migration overseas numbers, including "integrity, social cohesion and infrastructure adequacy, but meeting the needs of business must also be a key part of the considerations".

Both AiG and ACCI said migration is key to managing supply in the economy, and businesses remain in need of the skills new arrivals bring into the country.

"ACCI will continue to highlight the skills needs of employers and how business-related migration and international students bring broader benefits to the Australian community," Mr Alexander said.

The Property Council of Victoria says Australia needs skilled migrants (file photo). ( ABC News: Damien Larkins)

Country needs 'young tradies'

The Property Council of Australia argues the focus needs to be on the education of migrants who enter the country.

"The last two decades are a shocker in that only two in every 100 skilled migrants have had the construction skills for property projects a growing nation needs," chief executive Mike Zorbas said.

" We need young tradies, care workers and farm hands to support the levels of service our shrinking workforce, dwindling tax base and aging population demands. "

Mr Zorbas also thinks overseas student migration needs to be removed from the broader migration discussion.

"Carve students out of this debate," he said.

"They are here for an educational time, not a long time.

"We can easily provide the quality student accommodation they need close to unis if we just get the settings right."

Mr Taylor will deliver his budget reply speech at 7:30pm AEST on Thursday.

World.title: Bosisto's to triple eucalyptus oil production with new distillery
World.content:
Australian company Bosisto's has opened a new distillery in country Victoria, expanding its local production of eucalyptus oil.

The $10 million purpose-built facility near Wedderburn, north-west of Bendigo, triples the amount of oil the company can produce.

Eucalyptus oil is extracted from the leaves of blue mallee trees native to the area, using steam.

Bosisto's executive director, Tegan Abbott, said the new distillery is modern and efficient.

"We did previously have a distillery here, but [it was] pretty old and a little bit ancient," Ms Abbott said.

"We wanted to really set things up for new modern manufacturing capabilities, increase efficiencies, increase productivity, and also improve safety."

The historic, Australian-owned company has modernised its steam distillery. (Supplied: Bosisto's)

Eucalyptus oil has been used for its medicinal properties for thousands of years.

Pharmacist Joseph Bosisto pioneered the eucalyptus oil trade, establishing a commercial plantation and distillery in Victoria in 1852.

While Australia once supplied all of the world's eucalyptus oil, the local industry has declined in recent decades.

Bosisto's is now trying to reverse that.

"There's growing demand for eucalyptus oil out there," Ms Abbott said.

"Back in about 2011, we made a real investment to produce more eucalyptus oil, which required more eucalyptus trees.

"We embarked on quite a big project with Melbourne University to create high-yielding blue mallee trees, a bit like a super tree that could produce more oil."

Bosisto's is expanding its eucalyptus oil production in central Victoria. (Supplied: Bosisto's)

Five million trees were planted in central Victoria as part of that project.

"That's a lot of what we call leaf biomass that we want to distil … so we've built a new, a purpose-built facility for eucalyptus oil distillation," she said.

Ms Abbott said the new distillery will not only boost production by 300 per cent but also has sustainable features.

"We extract the oil from the leaf via steam distillation, and then that leaf biomass is actually used as fuel later on once it's dried out to stoke the boiler and create steam," she said.

"It's got off-grid capacity, so we've installed about 2,000 solar panels up here in order to power up the distillery, and then we're reusing a lot of water."

Bosisto's new distillery at Kurraca, near Wedderburn. (Supplied: Bosisto's)

The trees also re-grow after they are harvested.

"We cut a couple of centimetres from the ground … so we almost give them a haircut effectively," Ms Abbott said.

"We don't use pesticides or fertilisers. It's just rain, sun and the soil, and they continue to grow back up again."

Local manufacturing

The new distillery project was supported by the Victorian government through its Manufacturing Growth Program.

"Bosisto's is a long-running success story for regional Victoria," the Regional Development Minister Michaela Settle said.

"I'm thrilled that we've been able to support the next chapter, which will see a boost to regional production."

The Loddon Shire Council mayor, Dan Straub, said the investment was a vote of confidence in the region.

"Bosisto's have been a part of our strong local community for many decades," he said.

"[The facility] brings advanced manufacturing technology, new jobs and indirect economic activity for local businesses and suppliers."

At least seven new ongoing jobs have been created through the project, including five on-site.

Bosisto's used to use horse and cart to harvest eucalyptus leaves. (Supplied: Bosisto's)

Family legacy

The Bosisto's company has been owned by the Abbott family for 50 years.

Ms Abbott said her father, Peter Abbott, dreamt of seeing the Australian eucalyptus oil industry prosper before his death in 2022, aged 92.

"He was just really passionate about bringing it into the 21st century and modernising it," she said.

"When he first got involved, there were still horses and carts cutting trees.

"It feels like an accumulation of a lot of hard work, not just from him, but from our whole team."

The family plans to plant more trees and expand the business.

"That really is the plan … we'd love to see it continuing to grow," Ms Abbott said.

World.title: Court hears of horror stabbing that offender blames on Ozempic
World.content:
A sentencing hearing has been told of the pain and grief caused by a grandmother who stabbed her daughter-in-law and grandson during a roadside attack in the Illawarra last year.

The now 60-year-old offender, who cannot be named for legal reasons, admitted to forcing the family car to pull over at Wongawilli, south of Wollongong, before stabbing her 27-year-old daughter-in-law in the abdomen and her 10-year-old grandson in the neck.

She pleaded guilty to two counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm in April, but had previously told the court her actions may have been caused by the side effects of Ozempic.

Victim impact statements from the mother and a written letter from the grandchild were heard in court today, as other family members, including the offender's daughter, looked on.

"It's been a year of grief, pain and worry around me," the mother told the court via audiovisual link, with the faint cries of her newborn daughter heard in the background.

"I carry three scars on the side of my chest, which I try to conceal every day.

" There's also persistent images of holding my son's neck to stop the bleeding … meanwhile I was facing the reality that I may not survive. "

The 60-year-old woman was arrested by police at nearby Horsley the following morning and has been in custody since. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The court heard she had been unable to return to her job in the medical field due to the "presence of blood and sharp objects".

"I flinch at the drop of a spoon or if I touch a kitchen knife," the mother said.

" The psychological terror is implanted … it's a soul-shattering act that defies any moral standard. "

Wiping away tears, she went on to read comments written by her son in consultation with his psychologist.

"I didn't like how [my grandmother] ran to the car … she got me, and I felt something sharp," the court heard.

"I thought I was going to die."

"I miss my son's untainted look on life … the safety he once knew," the mother added.

Offender 'blacked out'

Dressed in prison greens and clenching a tissue, the offender appeared via audiovisual link from inside protective custody, where she has been for more than eight months.

She told the court she had no recollection of the attack, despite confessing to her son and daughter shortly after returning to her granny flat near the family home.

She did, however, admit to throwing the 15-centimetre fishing knife she used to stab her family members out of her car window while leaving the scene.

The matter was heard at Wollongong District Court on Thursday. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

"If that's what I told police, then yes," the offender told the court. "It's all a big blur. All I remember is getting back to the house."

While tendering documents, the defence told the court psychological experts had suggested the offender's violent actions may have been influenced by prescription weight-loss drugs.

"That's where this all began … I fell off the ladder at the granny flat, broke my arm, stopped smoking and went up to 90 kilograms, so my doctor gave me Ozempic," the offender said.

The Crown prosecutor told the court the offender asked which route the victims would be taking to judo practice and followed them with the intent to scare them.

"I do not accept evidence that she was simply curious … there was pre-planning here to some extent," she said.

Police searched a residential area of Wongawilli shortly after the alleged attack for a weapon. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Hunstdale)

The court heard black latex gloves worn during the incident were stored alongside the weapon inside the console of the offender's vehicle.

"They were for my cleaning job. I kept everything in my car," the offender said.

The court heard the offender misunderstood the grounds of a five-year apprehended violence order taken out by her son and his family, and penned an apology letter to him.

"I wanted to tell him how sorry I am, that I didn't know what I was doing, and that I love them all very much," she said.

Judge Imad Abdul-Karim will hand down his sentence in late June.

World.title: Breaking: Dozens injured in bus rollover on Queensland's Bruce Highway
World.content:
Dozens of passengers, some with life-threatening injuries, are being treated in a major emergency response to a bus rollover on Queensland's Bruce Highway.

The large coach crashed at Gumlu, between Townsville and Bowen, this afternoon.

Queensland Police arrived at the scene just after 4:30pm.

Queensland Ambulance Service (QAS) said 29 patients were being treated at the scene, two of those were in a life-threatening condition and the rest were stable.

QAS sent 11 crews and two rescue helicopters to the crash site.

The first patients are being transferred to hospital.

Police say the Bruce Highway is closed in both directions and warned motorists to avoid the area or expect long delays.

World.title: Who is in Trump's entourage of billionaires and executives in Beijing?
World.content:
US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are meeting in Beijing this week for a high-stakes two-day summit.

The "America-first" Republican has brought a select group of business titans, who have been snapped on the periphery of welcome events.

Here is what to know about who makes up the US delegation and why they've made the trans-Pacific trip.

Why is Trump in China?

Trade will be at the top of the summit's agenda.

Trump's "Freedom Day" tariffs sparked a tit-for-tat trade war with China last year.

The leader with the upper hand in Trump-Xi meeting Nine years after his last meeting with Xi Jinping in China, Donald Trump is more aggressive and assertive. But so is Beijing.

The US blocked shipments of the most advanced computer chips to China, and Beijing blasted back by periodically cutting off supplies of rare earth minerals crucial for batteries, medical devices and weapons manufacturing.

China stopped buying US soybeans, delivering a targeted blow to Trump's supporters in rural America.

Purchases resumed after talks between the US and China in October, but American soybean exports to China still dropped by 75 per cent in 2025.

Now, the two leaders are meeting to repair some of the damage.

Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will look to smooth trade relations during the summit. (Reuters: Kenny Holston/Pool)

Trump says he will be talking with Xi about trade "more than anything else".

Still, some other key issues are expected to dominate the agenda.

Taiwan Read more China is unhappy with US plans to sell weapons to Taiwan, a self-governing island the Chinese Communist Party claims as its own territory. On Monday, Trump told reporters he would discuss the $US11 billion ($15.16 billion) weapons package. The funding was authorised in December, but no money's been spent. The arms package is the largest the US has ever approved for Taiwan. Iran Read more With the world awaiting an end to the war in Iran, the conflict has already surfaced in the talks. China offered a veiled criticism of the US-led conflict in the Middle East back in April, urging the world not to revert to the "law of the jungle". Given its close political and economic ties with Iran, there have been suggestions it could influence Iranian leaders in ongoing peace talks. But China's cautious approach to the conflict indicates it would prefer to not get involved, according to experts. "I don't think China has any interest in solving the problems the US has created for itself in the Middle East," said Henrietta Levin, a senior fellow for the Freeman Chair in China Studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. A few days before the trip, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on China to pressure Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz, and said that by buying Iranian oil, Beijing was funding terrorism. "Let's see if China — let's see them step up with some diplomacy and get the Iranians to open the strait," Bessent said on Fox News. "Iran is the largest state sponsor of terrorism, and China has been buying 90 per cent of their energy, so they are funding the largest state sponsor of terrorism." But on his way to board Air Force One to fly to Beijing, Trump told reporters he did not think he needed help from Xi to end the war. "We have a lot of things to discuss," he said. "I wouldn't say Iran is one of them, to be honest with you, because we have Iran very much under control. "No, I don't think we need any help with Iran. We'll win it. We'll win it peacefully or otherwise."

Who is joining Trump in China?

When the president's private jet took off from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Tuesday, local time, Trump was not alone.

In addition to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Trump was joined by a handful of business executives.

Eric and Lara Trump Read more Eric Trump, the president's second-eldest son and the executive vice-president of the Trump Organization, was onboard Air Force One. He manages the company's global real estate portfolio, golf courses, and luxury hotels, alongside his older brother, Donald Trump Jr. The Trump Organization said the younger Trump was only in China to support his father, and there was no indication he would pursue business talks, according to the New York Times. Lara Trump, Eric's wife and the former co-chair of the Republican National Committee, was also on the flight. Jensen Huang Nvidia CEO Read more Trump personally invited Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to board Air Force One during a refuelling stop in Alaska on the way to Beijing. It comes just months after Nvidia received conditional approval to sell one of its powerful AI chips, the H200, to China. Those conditions allow the export of H200 chips, provided there is adequate supply in the US, and the H200 chips must undergo a third-party review before being exported to China. But these rules, set by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, lower the bar for chip exports to China. China won't be allowed to use the chips for military purposes and is not able to import more than 50 per cent of the chips sold to US customers. The H200 is not Nvidia's most advanced product. Those chips, called Blackwell and the upcoming Rubin, are not approved for export. Elon Musk Tesla and SpaceX CEO Read more Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX who led Trump's Department of Government Efficiency before it was shuttered in November, was on Air Force One, according to a White House official who spoke to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity. Just last year, the billionaire was in a war of words with Trump and claimed, without providing evidence, that the president was concealing information about his previous association with paedophile Jeffrey Epstein. Musk eventually said he regretted some of his comments. He has since refocused his energy on Tesla and his other companies. Brett Ratner Film director and producer Read more Reporters spotted Brett Ratner — who directed the Amazon documentary Melania, about first lady Melania Trump — on Air Force One. The filmmaker was effectively blacklisted from Hollywood, after multiple women accused him of sexual assault or misconduct in 2017. He has denied the allegations.

Trump said the following people were also among the group of business executives in China for the talks.

Apple CEO Tim Cook

Blackrock chairman and CEO Larry Fink

Blackstone chairman, CEO and co-founder Stephen Schwarzman

Boeing CEO Robert "Kelly" Ortberg

Cargill chairman and CEO Brian Sikes

Citi chairman and CEO Jane Fraser

GE Aerospace chairman and CEO H Lawrence Culp

Goldman Sachs chairman and CEO David Solomon

Micron chairman, president and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra

Qualcomm president and CEO Cristiano Amon

The US delegation awaiting the arrival of Donald Trump for a welcome ceremony at the Great Hall of the People on Thursday. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Why are the business executives there?

They will likely be seeking to negotiate investments and broker deals.

It's not unusual for business heads to tag along when US presidents make diplomatic trips, and major business deals or purchases are often announced during summit meetings between China and the US.

During his first term, Trump brought a delegation of corporate leaders on a trip to Beijing in 2017, and companies from the two nations signed trade and investment deals worth more than $US250 billion while there.

A signing ceremony during Donald Trump's visit to Beijing in 2017 saw the finalisation of $US250 billion in commercial agreements. (Reuters: Damir Sagolj)

Trump said he would ask Xi to give US firms greater access to the Chinese market, urging his Chinese counterpart to "'open up' China so that these brilliant people can work their magic".

Trump and Xi's AI talks will be critical for humanity When Trump last visited China in 2017, artificial intelligence was not yet the centre of global power. Now it is.

"In fact, I promise that when we are together, which will be in a matter of hours, I will make that my very first request," he wrote on Truth Social while travelling to Beijing.

"I have never seen or heard of any idea that would be more beneficial to our incredible Countries!"

As expected, the US and China have established a formal dialogue to guide their partnership over the coming years.

The two countries will establish a 'China-US Constructive Strategic Stability' as the new positioning of our relations," Xi said.

"This will provide strategic guidance for the next three years and beyond, and I believe it will be welcomed by both our peoples and the international community," according to a readout published by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

ABC/AP/Reuters

World.title: Trump and Xi meeting featured Taiwan, tech titans and flattery
World.content:
The first visit of a US president to China in nine years was always going to be a significant event, given the political and economic tensions between the two major superpowers in recent years.

Contentious issues, including the three Ts of trade, Tehran and Taiwan, loomed large over Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as they cut a path through Beijing.

But the pair, at least initially, appeared to be focused on projecting an aura of stability and friendlier ties.

That was clear from the very start of the high-stakes summit, when Trump stepped off Air Force One on Wednesday night and descended the stairs to a military honour guard at Beijing airport. Also waiting to greet the US leader was China's Vice-President, Han Zheng, and other officials.

Today, the pomp and ceremony continued as Trump and Xi met on the red carpet at the Great Hall of the People, before taking part in a bilateral meeting and a tour of the Temple of Heaven.

From a red carpet welcome to a high-profile tech entourage and a pointed reference to Taiwan, here are the main takeaways.

Beijing pulls out all the stops

In a sign of immense respect, Xi accompanied Trump to the Temple of Heaven.

The visit to the temple came after their bilateral meeting and signalled the relationship, and the event itself, was of great importance to Xi and China.

The leaders appeared to be making the most of an opportunity to stabilise relations, and these images from the temple visit suggest the day went relatively well.

Xi Jinping escorted US President Donald Trump on a tour of the Temple of Heaven in Beijing. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

China's state media had previously devoted considerable time to painting the United States as a reckless, chaotic and out-of-control superpower, but Trump didn't face the same level of criticism in the lead-up to his visit.

Observers believed this was a strategic decision to keep relations stable between the two leaders and to ensure the summit went as smoothly as possible.

Security and protective measures were also stepped up on the streets of Beijing this week to prevent any potential mishaps. Side streets were closed off, barriers put up and, in some areas, one guard was lined up every 15 metres.

Security has been beefed up across Beijing, including at Tiananmen Square. (Reuters: Go Nakamura)

Some of the media covering the event were caught out by the tighter security, with Fox News issued a ticket for parking on the street for too long. The ABC was also asked to move on by officials.

But there were no mishaps when Trump arrived at the Great Hall this morning to a red carpet lined with smiling children holding flowers and American flags.

The US leader seemed awed by the display as he met Xi with a long handshake and a brief chat, before posing for a photo.

One of the few awkward moments from the day's events occurred when a Chinese military band began playing the American anthem.

Donald Trump salutes while the US anthem is played. (AP)

Trump, who had been taking in the grand scene around him, raised his hand and saluted in front of the People's Liberation Army.

China's leader more reserved as Trump lavishes praise on Xi

Xi opened the talks with Trump in the Great Hall of the People by touching on the "Thucydides Trap", a popular theory that suggests an established power and a rising power are destined to clash.

Loading...

As he sat directly across from Trump in the centre of a long oval table, Xi noted: "The world has reached a new crossroads."

"Whether China and the United States can transcend the so-called Thucydides Trap and forge a new paradigm for engagement between major powers, whether we can work together to address global challenges and bring greater stability to the world, whether we can jointly create a brighter future for bilateral relations — these are questions of history, questions of the world, and questions of the people," he said.

The Chinese leader also said he had always believed that the "common interests shared by China and the United States far outweigh our differences".

"When the two sides cooperate, both benefit. When they confront each other, both suffer," he said.

Trump, meanwhile, spoke glowingly about the welcome ceremony he received and also the relationship between China and the US.

"It's an honour to be with you, it's an honour to be your friend, and the relationship between China and the USA is going to be better than ever before," he said.

He also heaped praise on his Chinese counterpart.

"You're a great leader. I say it to everybody. You're a great leader. Sometimes people don't like me saying it, but I say it anyway, because it's true," Trump added.

Xi issues a warning on Taiwan

During the bilateral meeting, Xi touched on the issue of Taiwan, according to China's state media CCTV.

"The Taiwan issue is the most critical issue in US-China relations," he said.

The island of Taiwan is democratically governed, claimed by China, and armed by the United States.

Chinese President Xi Jinping met US President Donald Trump on the red carpet at the Great Hall of the People, in Beijing. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

Earlier, Trump flagged that he would be discussing the sale of US weapons to Taiwan, saying: "President Xi would like us not to, and I'll have that discussion."

Today, Xi said relations between the two superpowers could remain stable if the issue of Taiwan was not "mishandled".

"If handled properly, bilateral relations can remain generally stable. If mishandled, the two countries will clash or even come into conflict, pushing the entire US-China relationship into a very dangerous situation," Xi warned.

"Taiwan independence and peace across the Taiwan Strait are fundamentally incompatible. Maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait is the greatest common denominator between China and the United States."

Taiwan's foreign minister Lin Chia-lung said he hoped the summit would "not produce any surprises" on issues relating to the island.

Trump's tech titan entourage

In keeping with Trump's preference to mix politics and business, even while abroad, the US president was joined in China by his inner circle — namely Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — as well as members of his family and a delegation of business leaders.

Some of them were familiar names from traditional American industries such as Blackrock's Larry Fink, Boeing's Kelly Ortberg, GE Aerospace's Lawrence Culp and Goldman Sachs's David Solomon.

But it was big-name tech leaders that drew considerable attention, including Apple chief executive Tim Cook, Space X billionaire Elon Musk, Meta's Dina Powell McCormick, and the head of chip giant Nvidia, Jensen Huang.

Space X and Tesla boss Elon Musk accompanied Donald Trump to Beijing. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

The choice of chief executives accompanying Trump was notable because they represented companies seeking to resolve business issues with China, particularly Nvidia.

US officials, cited by Reuters, said the business had struggled to get regulatory permission to sell its powerful H200 artificial intelligence chips there.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang was invited to Beijing for the meeting at the last minute. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

At the bilateral meeting at the Great Hall, some of the business delegation were welcomed inside, as Trump boasted about their presence to Xi while also noting they were there to "pay respects".

"We have the greatest business and the biggest, I guess. Best in the world. Amazing people, and they're all with me," he said in the Great Hall.

"We asked the top 30 in the world. Every single one of them said yes, and I didn't want the second or the third in the company, I wanted only the top, and they're here today to pay respects to you, China."

China talks of opening trade 'even wider'

Xi met with the American business entourage after talks with Trump and reportedly said US companies were deeply involved in his country's reform and its "opening up", according to state media agency Xinhua.

"China's door of opening up would only open wider," Xi said, adding that China welcomed stronger mutually beneficial cooperation with the US.

Trade was a big issue on the agenda ahead of Trump's visit. (Reuters: Brendan Smialowski)

He reportedly said he believed American companies would have broader prospects in China.

Behind closed doors, Xi said negotiations between economic and trade teams on Wednesday had reached an "overall balanced and positive outcome", according to Xinhua.

Both sides are eager to maintain the trade truce struck last October when Trump suspended triple-digit tariffs on Chinese goods and Xi backed away from choking global supplies of rare earths, vital in making items from electric cars to weapons, Reuters reported.

The US buys more from China than China buys from American firms, and that annoys Trump.

Washington wants to sell Boeing BA.N airplanes, farm goods and energy to China, while Beijing wants the US to ease curbs on exports of chipmaking equipment and advanced semiconductors, officials involved in the planning told Reuters.

And as the leaders met today, China renewed export licences for hundreds of US beef processing plants, opening the door for more American meat exports.

The comments from Xi on trade are potentially significant and surely what the business titans in the room wanted to hear. But the summit continues, and Xi was careful today to make sure all of this was underwritten by his warning on Taiwan.

Ahead of Trump's two-day visit, there was speculation that Iran would be a big focus for the two leaders, given the global effects of the conflict.

But the US president had sought to play that down before he left, telling reporters he doesn't need Xi to intervene in the Middle East crisis and said America doesn't "need any help with Iran".

Those comments might have been more telling than anyone realised, with very little mention of the war so far today.

World.title: China gives Trump a grand welcome and a stern warning on Taiwan
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations China gives Trump a grand welcome and a stern warning on Taiwan Lisa Visentin May 14, 2026 — 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: Welcomed with a red carpet ceremony of military pageantry and pomp, US President Donald Trump was effusive with praise for his Chinese counterpart and “great leader” Xi Jinping, who used the first talks of their two-day summit to send a warning about Taiwan. The world’s two most powerful men, keenly attuned to the optics of this high-stakes summit, projected an image of friendly rapport but had contrasting messages, before closing the doors at the Great Hall of the People to discuss the deep tensions that underpin the US-China relationship. Despite the cordial start to the summit, China’s President Xi Jinping warned Trump that the issue of Taiwan could push their two countries into “conflict” if mishandled. AP More restrained than his American rival, Xi said that the two countries stood to benefit from co-operation and should be “partners and not rivals”, adding that “when we confront each other, both sides suffer,” in brief remarks that were open to media. But behind closed doors, he delivered a warning to Trump over Taiwan, which he described as the “most important issue” shaping the future of China-US ties.



“If mishandled, the two nations will experience collision or even clashes, pushing the entire China-US relationship into a highly dangerous situation,” Xi said, according to a readout by China’s state-run Xinhua news agency. Loading Before this occurred, Trump – the first US president to make a state visit to China in nearly a decade – lavished praise on Xi during his opening remarks, saying it was “an honour to be your friend”. “I say it to everybody, you’re a great leader. Sometimes people don’t like me saying it. But I say it anyway because it’s true,” he said, noting he had brought top US executives with him “to pay respects to you and to China”. Accompanying Trump’s delegation is Tesla’s Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook, among other business leaders, including from Boeing, which is expected to secure more Chinese purchase orders of its jets at the summit.



The summit kicked off with a spectacle on the forecourt of the Great Hall, the prestigious building used for China’s legislature and ceremonial events, with Xi descending the steps to greet Trump with a handshake. They then walked a red carpet together, inspecting an honour guard, and pausing to admire groups of cheering children waving flags and flowers. At one point, the US anthem played as a 21-gun salute echoed across Tiananmen Square. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in Beijing. AP, Getty Images Inside the building, Trump touted their meeting as “maybe the biggest summit ever” and predicted the US-China relationship “is going to be better than ever before”. But his rosy assessment comes against a more sobering backdrop of a simmering trade feud, a race to dominate artificial intelligence, and friction over Taiwan, plus the added tension of the Iran war, all of which has intensified the two countries’ competition for power and prestige on the world stage.



Chinese and Western analysts have low expectations that the summit will secure major outcomes much beyond extending the trade truce sealed by Trump and Xi during their last meeting in South Korea in October, and more commitments by China to buy US goods. Related Article Analysis

China relations The ‘big danger’ for Australia as Trump meets Xi “Both Xi and Trump need the optics right now,” said Ja Ian Chong, an expert in Chinese foreign policy at the National University of Singapore. “Xi is facing domestic economic headwinds, wants to show some sort of ‘win’ – that he’s a big, powerful leader and Trump is a very useful prop to that end.” Trump is also looking to lock in “wins”, arriving in Beijing under pressure to end the Iran war, which has caused a global oil shock and hammered his popularity back home. His tariff regime is also in tatters after a key component was ruled illegal by the US courts.



He is expected to announce new deals that will see China buy more American agricultural products, energy, beef, and jets, and establish a “Board of Trade” to oversee those commitments. It is not yet clear whether any deals were agreed on the first day of talks, which lasted about two hours. Xi and Trump later toured the Temple of Heaven, a 15th-century world heritage site used by Ming and Qing dynasty emperors to offer sacrifices and pray for good harvests. China’s President Xi Jinping (centre), US President Donald Trump and Eric Trump at the Temple of Heaven in Beijing. Getty Images Xi will host Trump at a banquet on Thursday evening, before further talks at Zhongnanhai, the Chinese leadership compound. Before his arrival in Beijing, Trump said he anticipated speaking with Xi about US arms sales to Taiwan, with the Chinese leader expected to press him to reduce or end the military support to the democratic island.



This has triggered speculation that Trump could agree to scale back support for Taiwan, either militarily or rhetorically, in exchange for Xi using China’s influence on Iran to help end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Beijing buys 90 per cent of Iranian oil, making it a key financial lifeline for the Islamic Republic. Speaking on Air Force One while on route to China, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that China’s relationship with Iran would be on the agenda, though he made no link to Taiwan. US officials have previously downplayed suggestions Trump will make any changes to Taiwan policy. “It’s in [China’s] interest to resolve this, and we hope to convince them to play a more active role in getting Iran to walk away from what they’re doing now and trying to do now in the Persian Gulf,” Rubio told Fox News’ Sean Hannity. Loading



Wu Xinbo, director of the Centre for American Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said China certainly had some influence with Iran, but it was unlikely Xi and Trump would find common ground on how that influence should be used. Related Article Opinion

China relations Trump burnt Xi last time. Today, he needs the Chinese president to save him Clinton Fernandes Academic and former intelligence officer “When the US asks China to help to exert some influence, it usually means you should embrace our position and exert pressure on Iran. That’s not the way we think we should exercise our influence,” Wu said. Chong said the Taiwan card would be a big concession by the US, but he doubted Beijing’s influence over Iran was sufficient to get the result Trump wanted, such as abandoning its nuclear weapons program. “Beijing might be able to do things on the margins, but on things that are pretty fundamental to Tehran’s position, I’m not sure even Beijing has the wherewithal to persuade Iran,” he said. World.title: Strict new criteria, sweeping ministerial powers: All the changes coming for NDIS
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDisability Strict new criteria, sweeping ministerial powers: All the changes coming for NDIS Natassia Chrysanthos Updated May 14, 2026 — 6:01pm ,first published 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor’s new laws to limit who can access the National Disability Insurance Scheme will give the responsible minister sweeping powers to make mass cuts to budgets or therapies and enable automated decision-making, in efforts to cut spending by $38 billion in four years. Health Minister Mark Butler’s bill to restrict who can join the $56 billion NDIS, introduced on Thursday, will require people to have exhausted all other treatment options before they are considered permanently impaired to enter the scheme. Broad ministerial powers will allow Butler to put an instant break on certain parts of the scheme if costs start spiralling, but the minister assured participants that any automation would be carefully considered and focus on administrative tasks, as he sought to allay fears of a “Robodebt” scenario. Mark Butler during a press conference at Parliament House in Canberra on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen/image digitally tinted These laws are crucial for the government to action its NDIS overhaul and recoup around $170 billion in a decade. More than half the $64 billion savings banked in Tuesday’s budget assume NDIS eligibility and spending will be drastically curtailed within four years.



But Labor’s plans immediately hit a hurdle on Thursday when the Senate sent the bill to an inquiry, due to report by June, and the Greens declared it “one of the most dangerous pieces of legislation that has ever been put forward by our government in relation to disabled people”. “This new bill makes massive, significant changes to the NDIS that will make life harder for disabled people across the country,” said Greens disability spokesman Jordon Steele-John. “It also grants the minister vast new powers, which they do not have today, to make massive changes to the supports that disabled people and our families have in place right now. And they can make those decisions while sitting behind a desk in Canberra without ever having to talk to you.” The government will need the Coalition’s support to pass the bill. “The Coalition will review the bill carefully and consult with the disability community through the Senate inquiry, which I think is an important part of the process,” said spokeswoman Melissa McIntosh.



NDIS blowouts have eroded Labor’s bottom line as wide eligibility criteria, loose regulation and vague legal definitions have allowed the scheme’s costs to grow by more than 10 per cent a year. The overhaul aims to restore it to its original purpose so it grows at 5 per cent in future. “The NDIS was intended to operate as a targeted, insurance-based scheme for people with permanent and significant disability,” the bill’s explanatory document, published Thursday, said. “It is not intended to operate as an unconstrained funding source for all disability-related needs, nor should it be used to address supports that would be more appropriately provided by other service systems.” Up to 300,000 people will be removed from the scheme when eligibility changes come in from January 2028. Tuesday’s budget papers show annual NDIS funding will go backwards to $55 billion as changes roll out, before returning to $56.2 billion in 2029-30. New laws reveal first steps to eligibility changes



The bill clarifies that someone’s “functional capacity” is assessed on whether they can perform an activity without help from other people, technology or modifications – it does not consider personal circumstances, such as their financial means or living arrangements. It also clarifies how “permanent impairments” are defined, saying someone must have explored all other appropriate treatments before accessing the scheme. “An impairment cannot be found to be permanent if there is any other treatment which is likely to materially improve, reverse, or alleviate the impact,” the explanation says. “To be found permanent, the person’s impairment or impairments are likely to persist for the person’s lifetime.” The laws will tighten eligibility for the NDIS if there are other supports or services that could meet someone’s needs. These include if someone can access workers compensation or motor vehicle accident compensation schemes, affecting an estimated 8000 participants. “This scheme was never set up to become a substitute for health and rehabilitation and other treatment that could potentially prevent lifelong disability, so we will put in place rules that that make that much clearer,” Butler said on Thursday.



“We won’t, for example, require people with profound hearing loss to receive a cochlear implant. There will be exceptions to that question of treatment, and the detail of that will be developed.” The laws will also confirm people can only access NDIS support for needs that arise directly from their qualifying impairment. This means that someone with cerebral palsy using the scheme, for example, cannot get support for ADHD or dyslexia. Related Article Analysis

Disability NDIS overhaul is the biggest government cut this century. It had better work These changes will override court and tribunal decisions that have expanded the NDIS’ scope, as well as the automatic “access lists” that currently guarantee people can enter the scheme with diagnoses such as level two or three autism. A technical advisory group will give the government advice on the appropriate thresholds and assessments for eligibility, and it will be informed by community consultation.



Sweeping powers give minister control over spending Thursday’s laws also give the minister new powers to make blunt cuts that limit either how much money is allocated, or how many supports can be accessed, in certain sections of the NDIS. “These determinations are not applied on a ‘plan-by-plan’ basis, but rather have the effect of reducing the funding for certain groups of supports across the scheme,” the explanation said. This measure is designed to allow the minister to “directly manage the financial sustainability of the scheme”, and any changes to people’s funding as a result will not be subject to merits reviews. Butler last month said he would use this power to cull people’s social and community participation budgets, which tripled to $12 billion in five years. He will reset this funding at 2023 levels to quickly cut spending.



“I also intend to reset the therapy budgets, which on average, will mean... a shift from around 71 or 72 hours of therapy a year, down to about 68 hours of therapy per year,” he said on Thursday. The minister will gain powers to set prices, instead of the National Disability Insurance Agency, and Butler plans to pay registered providers more for the same service than unregistered providers. Related Article Exclusive

Disability New NDIS eligibility tool will be ‘relatively blind’ to diagnoses: Butler Laws tackling fraud will enable new civil penalties and give the National Disability Insurance Agency powers to investigate criminal activity. Providers and participants will have to keep records for specified periods of time, and make claims within 90 days of a support being provided. They also enable other changes Butler announced last month, such as clamping down on unscheduled plan reassessments that have been a key driver of NDIS inflation, and moving to a system where the government decides what plan managers people can use.

World.title: Snowy Hydro bracing for 10-fold cost blowout
World.content:
PoliticsFederalEnergy Snowy Hydro bracing for 10-fold cost blowout Andrew Probyn May 14, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The operators of Snowy Hydro 2.0 are bracing for a more than 10-fold cost blowout in the mega project that is already running seven years behind schedule. But the federal government remains committed to the renewable energy project, which is now two-thirds complete. Loading This masthead visited Snowy 2.0 at an important milestone, the breakthrough of tunnel boring machine Eileen into a cavern deep underground and the completion of her six-kilometre section of the tunnelling task. Florence, the tunnel-boring machine that infamously got stuck for 11 months just 150 metres into her dig, is now seven kilometres into her 15-kilometre task, with project director Dave Evans confident she can reach boring speeds of 90 days for every remaining kilometre.



“The logistics of getting deep underground to build such a big power station comes with challenges, and that’s what we’re here for,” Evans said. “This project that we’re building will last 150 years, so it’s going to be here for a hell of a long time.” All up, 19 kilometres of the project’s 27 kilometres of tunnels have been bored. When completed, Snowy 2.0 promises to be Australia’s biggest battery, storing the equivalent of 26 million home batteries by using excess solar and wind energy to pump water into the upper Tantangara reservoir for release when power is needed.



This masthead visited the enormous cavern nearly one kilometre below the surface that will house a six-turbine generator. The 200-metre-long cavern is big enough to fit the Sydney Opera House, and at 67 metres tall, could comfortably fit the Leaning Tower of Pisa. But the spiralling cost of Snowy 2.0 remains problematic. Eileen breaks through a cavern wall after boring a six-kilometre tunnel. SnowyHydro When then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull announced Snowy Hydro 2.0 in 2017, it was given a price tag of $2 billion and a completion date of 2021. The projected cost escalated to $6 billion, then lifted to $12 billion in 2023, with Snowy Hydro chief executive Dennis Barnes conceding this figure will be exceeded and the completion date pushed back to late 2028.



“We’re not going to get it done for $12 billion so we’ve asked our contractor to do a line-by-line assessment, which they’re due to complete in the next couple of weeks,” Barnes said. Sources with knowledge of the project unable to speak publicly told this masthead that the project’s latest price tag will be about $22 billion – 11 times the original estimate. Barnes defended the blowout, saying the project was “one of the most complex engineering projects underway in the world” that demanded millimetre precision in a remote part of Kosciuszko National Park. “The announcements in the early days were all pre-feasibility stage. Obviously, as you do more, you learn more. And progressively, over the last 10 years or so, we’ve gone through a few stages where we’ve understood more,” he said. “Although there was the famous $2 billion by 2021 announced, no work had been done at that point.



“When we got to about 40 per cent of the way through the project, three years ago, we reset the project. We said when it was going to finish, and we said how much it was going to cost. Now, some of those have proven wrong, but until you do the work, you don’t really know.” Related Article Exclusive

Electricity Leaked videos reveal flooding in troubled Snowy 2.0 tunnel project Economist Bruce Mountain and energy executive Ted Woodley last month claimed the true cost of the project would be $42 billion, but Barnes said this was inaccurate. “That number … includes interest costs, which are nowhere near the interest costs we face as a company [and] it includes the cost of transmission, which has got nothing to do with this project.”



The Mountain-Woodley estimate includes $8 billion in interest and $12 billion as Snowy’s share of transmission costs, both figures Barnes contests. “Now we will connect into those transmission projects, but the cost of those transmission projects are not part of this project,” he said. One of the major financial pressure points for the project is labour and associated logistical costs such as fly-in-fly-out arrangements, accommodation and meals. Workers on the tunnel boring machines are paid more than $300,000 under a two-weeks-on, one-week-off arrangement. Last week, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the Albanese government was committed to the project, notwithstanding the fact that the “incoming government had to deal with the consequences of that poorly scoped, poorly designed project”.



“It is a huge, massive infrastructure undertaking and it has encountered several challenges that were not understood at the point that the project was approved by the former government. We’re working through all of those issues, as you’d expect.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Fixture reveal: How Spud’s Game could be impetus for more Sunday night footy
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Fixture reveal: How Spud’s Game could be impetus for more Sunday night footy Andrew Wu Updated May 14, 2026 — 5:59pm ,first published 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Click here for the AFL fixture or scroll down for our interactive St Kilda’s special “Spud’s Game” against Carlton is being used as a trial by the AFL for more Sunday night football, as the league explores non-traditional time slots for games. Head office has a major supporter for Sunday night football in broadcast partner Seven, which, enthused by the growth in year-on-year ratings, is keen to see more games in the time slot. The league generally avoids scheduling matches on Sunday nights unless it falls on the eve of a public holiday but made an exception for the round 22 game between the Saints and the Blues in the latest release of the fixture on Thursday. St Kilda, Carlton and the umpires link arms before Spud’s Game in 2025. AFL Photos



The AFL is not seeking to make Sunday night footy a regular fixture but, according to an industry source with direct knowledge of the matter, is keen to test interest among fans and viewers. The match will be broadcast on Seven, in place of their usual Sunday game at 3.15pm (AEST) leading into their most-watched news bulletin of the week. Sunday night is the highest-rating evening for free-to-air TV, when networks show their tent pole programs that hold up their audience for the week, and has not traditionally been seen as the time for live sport, but Seven are embracing the possibility of more games. “2026 has delivered more Sunday night prime-time games than ever before and has delivered a strong ratings lift year-on-year, on Seven and 7plus,” Seven’s head of AFL and sport innovation Gary O’Keeffe said in a statement to this masthead.



“Having Spud’s Game in prime time on a Sunday night, broadcast on free to air, gives the landmark occasion the platform it deserves.



“We’re excited by the momentum Sunday night footy continues to build and will continue to work with the AFL to ensure live and free Sunday night footy can become a mainstay on Seven and 7plus Sport.” “Spud’s Game”, held in honour of late St Kilda legend Danny Frawley, is the Blues’ only prime-time match from rounds 16 to 22 as the league turns its back on failing powerhouses Carlton and Essendon for Thursday and Friday night footy in favour of the premiership contenders. Fallen giants Carlton and Essendon have been scrubbed from prime time. Getty Images Ladder leaders Sydney, back-to-back premiers Brisbane Lions and perennial finalists Geelong all feature on the coveted prime-time free to air TV slots in the league’s schedule from rounds 16-22. Even Fremantle and the pioneers of night football, the Kangaroos, have been given the nod ahead of the Blues and Bombers.



The AFL has learnt the lessons from last year’s fixture misjudgment by turning its back on the under-performing Melbourne giants. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Swans abandon Pride Game plans with Saints after Lance Collard case AFL fixture boss Josh Bowler was blunt in explaining the snubbing of the Bombers and Blues. “They’re both currently sitting in the bottom four on the ladder,” Bowler said. “We generally won’t have bottom-four type match-ups in prime time.” Not even the Blues’ clash with arch-rival Collingwood was deemed worthy of free-to-air TV.



The Bombers have become Sunday specialists with five matches on that day, including three in the graveyard 4.40pm start. The AFL is backing in the box office appeal of the Swans by handing them four Thursday and Friday night matches, including the opening game of round 16 against the Lions. “The Showdown” in Adelaide, arguably the league’s biggest rivalry, has been given its own time slot but not on a Thursday or Friday night, instead scheduled as the only Saturday night game in round 16. The league has given Hawthorn and GWS the Friday night match in that round. Highlighting head office’s faith in non-Victorian clubs, Fremantle and the Swans will kick off proceedings in round 18 in a game that could go a long way towards deciding which of those clubs snares a crucial top-two finish. This is one of three Thursday and Friday night games featuring two clubs outside of Victoria. “When you’ve got top teams competing for finals, I think footy fans will watch their Victorian teams over the weekend, but see the games of consequence happening on a Thursday, Friday nights,” Bowler said.



The Lions have been recognised for their continued excellence with three prime-time games, against fellow flag contenders Sydney, Geelong and Hawthorn. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 One rule, a century of chaos: Why we still can’t define holding the ball Wayne Campbell Age columnist and former Richmond captain The Kangaroos, who made Friday night football their own in the 1980s and ’90s, play Collingwood in their first standalone game in that time slot since 2019, in a move that recognises North’s rise out of the doldrums. Alastair Clarkson’s men also have a round 22 Thursday night clash against the Western Bulldogs, which could be pivotal in deciding a finals berth. “I think they’ll at the very least be competing for a wildcard spot,” Bowler said.



Bowler said the inaugural set of wildcard finals will be held on Friday and Saturday nights. The AFL is holding off its scheduling for rounds 23 and 24. Richmond’s mighty tumble has been underlined with just one match on free to air, against Melbourne on the Sunday of round 18. Friday night double-headers are here to stay, but the league refused to commit to them becoming a regular part of the fixture, saying it would treat them on a “case-by-case basis”. There are two Friday night double-headers, in rounds 17 and 20, the latter involving the Western Derby. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

Multiple people have been injured and two are in life-threatening condition after a bus crash in north Queensland.

Emergency services were called to the vehicle – which had 29 people on board – on the Bruce Highway at Gumlu, about 90 minutes south of Townsville, at 4pm.

The Queensland Ambulance Service said everyone on board was assessed for injuries. Two were in a life-threatening condition.

Helicopters were flown in from Mackay and Townsville, with the first patients transported to hospital just after 5pm.
